opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. RETRO came out of a fairly simple question we were asking at DeepMind: does every piece of knowledge a model uses really need to be stored in its parameters? If you train a huge dense model, you're paying in compute and memory to memorize a lot of facts, a lot of surface-level text, that you could in principle just look up.

So the idea was to separate two things: the reasoning and language-modeling capacity, which lives in the weights, and the factual knowledge, which can live in an external database. With RETRO we retrieved chunks from a very large corpus, trillions of tokens, and let the model attend to those neighbors while it was predicting the next token. What we saw was that a relatively small model with retrieval could match much larger models on some language-modeling benchmarks. That told us parameters aren't the only lever you have.

It fit into a broader line of thinking for me, which was really about efficiency. Around the same time we were working on scaling laws, the Chinchilla work, which showed that most large models were undertrained relative to their size and that you should balance parameters and data much more carefully. Retrieval and compute-optimal training come from the same instinct: be careful about where you spend your compute, and don't assume bigger is automatically better.

To be honest, retrieval inside pretraining turned out to be operationally complicated. You have to maintain the index, deal with leakage between training and evaluation data, and the serving story is harder. Where the idea really survived is at inference time, in retrieval-augmented generation, where you plug a model into a company's documents or a search system. That's very much how we think about it at Mistral. You want a compact, efficient model that reasons well, and then you connect it to the knowledge it needs instead of trying to cram everything into the weights. That makes the model cheaper to run, easier to update, and much more useful for enterprises whose data changes every day.

r001.rationale: The response says RETRO retrieved corpus chunks for next-token prediction, and explicitly discusses retrieval during pretraining. It also explains that factual knowledge can live in an external database instead of being stored in the model’s weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, RETRO came out of a very simple observation we had at DeepMind, which is that we were spending enormous amounts of compute just to memorize facts inside the weights of the model. A lot of the parameters in a large language model are essentially a lossy database. So the question was, why not separate the two things? Keep the parameters for reasoning and language, and put the knowledge somewhere it can be looked up.

So what we did was give the model access to a very large corpus, trillions of tokens, through a retrieval mechanism. At each chunk of text the model would go fetch nearby passages from this database and attend to them through a cross-attention layer. And the result was that a model with something like twenty-five times fewer parameters could match the performance of much larger models on perplexity. That was quite striking to us at the time.

For me it fit very naturally with the way I think about efficiency, which is really about not wasting compute on things that don't need to be learned. It's the same spirit as the Chinchilla work, where we showed people were training models that were too big for the amount of data they had. In both cases the lesson is the same: the frontier isn't just about scale, it's about allocating resources intelligently. Retrieval is one way of doing that, mixture of experts is another, better data is another.

Now, I'll be honest, RETRO also showed us the limits. Retrieval is very good for factual recall, but the model still has to know how to reason, how to follow instructions, how to compose things. You can't retrieve your way to intelligence. So at Mistral we've focused a lot on making the core model as dense in capability as possible per parameter, and then letting retrieval, tools, and context be things the developer adds on top. That separation of concerns is something I took directly from that period.

r001.rationale: The response explains that RETRO used retrieval from an external corpus to reduce knowledge stored in model parameters, but it does not say this access occurred during pretraining.

astra-6.text:
The idea with RETRO was to ask whether everything a language model knows really needs to be stored in its parameters. You can instead give it access to an external memory—a large collection of text—and train it to retrieve relevant passages and use them when predicting what comes next.

That gives you another way to increase capacity without simply making the neural network bigger. The model’s parameters can focus more on learning how to use information, while some of the factual content lives outside the model. There is still a cost to retrieval, of course, but it opens up a different tradeoff between model size, computation, and access to knowledge. That was the efficiency question that interested me.

r001.rationale: The response says RETRO retrieves passages from external text and keeps some facts outside the model’s parameters, but it does not clearly say this access happens during pretraining.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea behind RETRO was to ask whether a model really needs to store all of its knowledge in its parameters. We gave it access to an external collection of text, so it could retrieve relevant passages and use them as it generated an answer. The parameters could then focus more on processing information and less on memorizing facts.

That was interesting from an efficiency perspective because you could get strong performance with a smaller model by giving it more information at inference time. Of course, retrieval has a cost as well, so you’re trading some parameter compute for looking things up. But it opened up a different way to scale: improving the memory the model can access, rather than only making the model itself bigger.

r001.rationale: The response says RETRO retrieved passages from an external text collection while generating answers and reduced the need to memorize facts in parameters. It does not say this access occurred during pretraining.
